analysis.one_liner: Lets victims of fake AI-generated sexual images sue the people who create and share them.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed it unanimously by voice vote in July 2024, but the House never voted on it and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let any identifiable person sue whoever knowingly made, shared, or solicited an AI-generated fake sexual image of them, even if a label says it is fake. Victims could win up to $250,000 in fixed damages, the wrongdoer's profits, attorney fees, and court orders deleting the images. It also extends the deadline to sue to 10 years, and protects victims' privacy in court. The Senate passed it without opposition, but it never received a vote in the House.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose likeness is pasted into a fake nude or sexual image — a growing problem since cheap apps now let anyone create realistic fakes with no technical skill [S3]. The bill's own findings describe victims suffering harassment, extortion, depression, and withdrawal from public life, and say labeling content as fake does not fix the harm [S3]. Victims would gain a practical legal weapon: money damages, the wrongdoer's profits, attorney fees to make lawsuits affordable, and injunctions forcing deletion of the images [S3]. Special provisions protect minors and let plaintiffs sue under a pseudonym so the lawsuit itself does not publicize the abuse [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of AI fake sexual images

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal civil lawsuit right for anyone depicted in a nonconsensual AI 'deepfake' sexual image, against people who knowingly produced, disclosed, solicited, or possessed it with intent to distribute [S2].
Victims can recover fixed damages of $150,000, or $250,000 when the fake was tied to sexual assault, stalking, or harassment, plus the wrongdoer's profits and attorney fees [S3].

Courts can order images deleted or destroyed, shield the victim's identity with a pseudonym and sealed filings, and the statute of limitations runs 10 years from discovery or the victim's 18th birthday, whichever is later [S3].
The bill counts a fake as a forgery even if it is labeled as fake, closing the loophole where platforms disclaim responsibility by tagging AI content [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The people and businesses who make or traffic in these images: anyone who knowingly produces, shares, or solicits nonconsensual deepfake sexual imagery can be sued for damages, the defendant's profits, and fees, and operators of sites or apps profiting from such content face losing those profits and paying fixed awards up to $250,000 per victim [S3].

drawbacks.text: Critics of aggressive deepfake regulation argue broad civil liability could chill lawful activity — artists, satirists, and AI tool developers could face costly lawsuits over images that someone else deems 'indistinguishable from authentic,' though the bill requires the depiction to be sexual or nude in nature and knowingly nonconsensual [S3].
The remedies focus on civil damages, which only help victims who can identify the defendant; many victims cannot determine who created the content, as the bill's own findings concede [S3].
As a civil bill it imposes no criminal penalty on the underlying conduct, leaving enforcement to private lawsuits that victims must fund and win [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are substantial and directly targeted: it hands real, money-backed remedies to people who today have little recourse when cheap AI tools are used against them. The main honest concerns are litigation risk for people who might unknowingly touch unlawful content, and the fact that damages only work if the wrongdoer can be found and identified — a limit the bill itself acknowledges. On balance the design is protective rather than overbroad, and it explicitly does not preempt stronger state laws [S3].

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it unanimously by voice vote on July 23, 2024, but after the House received it the next day, it was simply held at the desk — nobody ever brought it up for a vote, and it expired when the Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Durbin introduced the bill in the Senate on January 30, 2024, and it was referred to the Judiciary Committee [S5].
Eight senators from both parties signed on as cosponsors — 3 Republicans, 4 Democrats, and 1 Independent [S4].
On July 23, 2024, the Judiciary Committee released the bill and the Senate passed it with an amendment by voice vote, meaning no senator objected and no recorded roll call was taken [S5].
The House received the bill on July 24, 2024, and held it at the desk; no committee referred it and no vote ever occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The people who create, host, or profit from nonconsensual fake sexual images are better off, because they never faced the civil liability and profit clawbacks the bill would have imposed. House leadership, which never scheduled a vote on a bill the Senate passed unanimously, decided the outcome.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Deepfake creators and the platforms hosting them

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan support.

for.what_they_did: Discharged the bill by unanimous consent on July 23, 2024, allowing immediate Senate consideration.

against.name: House leadership
against.role: Speaker and House majority leadership, 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on July 24, 2024 and left it 'held at the desk' for five months, never scheduling committee action or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There is no recorded opposition anywhere: the Senate passed it by voice vote with an evenly bipartisan set of cosponsors (3 Republicans, 4 Democrats, 1 Independent), and no House vote ever occurred to reveal a partisan split [S4][S5].

industries.note: The technology is now cheap and ubiquitous, with hundreds of apps that generate fake nudes with no technical expertise; the bill would expose anyone knowingly producing such images to lawsuits with fixed damages up to $250,000. Its death leaves this market free of the liability the Senate unanimously approved [S3].

industries.industry: Websites and platforms that host or profit from intimate image content
industries.note: The bill targets distributors, solicitors, and those possessing images with intent to distribute, and lets victims recover the defendant's profits, so sites earning money from nonconsensual deepfakes could have been stripped of that revenue. Some platforms would also have faced pressure to take down content or face injunctions ordering deletion [S3].
